strengths: OccuFly addresses a valuable gap in aerial semantic scene completion. Its 20,160 image–occupancy pairs, metric depth maps, 22 semantic classes, and scene-disjoint splits could support research beyond existing terrestrial benchmarks.

The camera-based annotation pipeline is practically motivated and clearly structured. Combining reconstruction, multi-view label transfer, and class-aware densification reduces direct 3D annotation requirements; Table 8 documents 586 annotated images among 6,393 acquisition images.

The depth estimation experiment demonstrates useful in-domain supervision: fine-tuning Depth Anything V2 improves AbsRel from approximately 0.69–0.77 to 0.10–0.15 across the three altitudes (Table 4).

The supplement provides useful implementation parameters, per-scene reconstruction statistics, class frequencies, and qualitative outputs. The manuscript also explicitly acknowledges static-scene assumptions and temporal inconsistencies between altitude captures.
weaknesses: Ground-truth accuracy is insufficiently established for a benchmark whose central contribution is its generated labels. The reported 1.24-pixel reprojection error measures internal reconstruction consistency; it does not establish absolute metric depth accuracy, semantic correctness, or completion accuracy. Likewise, covering over 99% of reconstructed points does not measure annotation correctness or coverage of missing geometry. No independent geometric reference or quantitative audit of transferred and densified labels is reported. This is the principal concern determining the weak-reject recommendation.

The occupancy construction can conflate missing evidence with empty space. Equation (13) assigns empty labels wherever the reconstruction and densification produce no occupied voxel, while the invalid mask in Section 3.3.4 excludes only regions outside the viewing frustum. Thus, unobserved or unreconstructed regions inside it are not explicitly distinguished from verified free space. Virtual silhouettes derived from the same incomplete point cloud and Poisson hole filling introduce additional geometric assumptions, but their accuracy and effects on benchmark scores are not quantified.

The SSC baseline does not adequately resolve whether poor results reflect aerial task difficulty or problems with model adaptation and supervision. CGFormer obtains only 0.0080 mIoU and 0.2406 occupancy IoU overall (Table 11), with zero scores for numerous classes. There is no simple reference baseline, ground-truth-depth diagnostic, or training/convergence evidence to contextualize this near-collapse. Low performance itself is not a reason to reject a dataset, but the present evidence does not substantiate the broader conclusions about existing SSC architectures.

Several experimental interpretations exceed the evidence. Class-frequency correlations do not establish that CGFormer would perform well under near-uniform class distributions (Section 5.2). Table 10 compares reciprocal transfer on different target datasets, so differences in absolute errors cannot establish superior cross-domain generalization; furthermore, DAv2-OccuFly has worse AbsRel in that comparison, contrary to the broad claim about metric-sensitive measures.

The effective diversity is substantially narrower than the sample count suggests: nine scenes from one geographic region, with only two test scenes and no rural test scene. Buildings account for 75.75% of occupied labels, while several advertised classes are extremely rare. These limitations restrict conclusions about geographic, seasonal, and fine-grained semantic generalization, particularly without per-scene results.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful supplementary parameters. The precise transformation and origin used to sample camera-associated grids from the global voxel grid are underspecified, and the depth fine-tuning schedule is not fully documented. These are correctable reporting issues, but they matter when interpreting unusually low SSC performance.

strengths: OccuFly addresses a meaningful gap in aerial semantic scene completion. Its 20,160 image–occupancy pairs, metric depth maps, 22 semantic classes, and scene-disjoint splits could provide a useful resource for an underexplored computer vision task.

The camera-based annotation pipeline is practically motivated. Combining photogrammetric reconstruction, sparse 2D annotation, label propagation, and class-aware voxelization reduces dependence on specialized aerial LiDAR acquisition. Table 8 documents 586 annotated images out of 6,393 reconstruction images, supporting annotation efficiency.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, including clustering parameters, reconstruction settings, class frequencies, and training hardware. Scene-level visualizations help explain the resulting annotations.

The depth experiments demonstrate a concrete benefit from in-domain supervision: Table 4 reports substantial improvements over terrestrial DAv2-metric at every altitude, with AbsRel decreasing from 0.693–0.767 to 0.103–0.148.
weaknesses: The central concern is insufficient validation of the benchmark ground truth. Sections 4.3 and 8 use a 1.24-pixel reprojection RMSE to support metric geometry and depth accuracy, but reprojection consistency does not independently establish metric scale, surface accuracy, or completeness. Likewise, correspondence coverage measures whether points receive labels, not whether those labels are correct. There is no quantitative independent audit of geometry, semantic transfer, or the completed occupancy labels. This is consequential for a paper whose principal contribution is a benchmark.

The occupancy construction introduces substantial unvalidated assumptions. Instance occupancy comes from silhouettes synthesized from the reconstructed point cloud, ground occupancy from Poisson reconstruction, and other classes from direct voxelization. These operations can impose different completeness and shape biases across classes. Equation (13) labels remaining voxels empty, while Equation (14) excludes only voxels outside the frustum; unreconstructed regions inside it are therefore not distinguished from verified free space. The paper does not quantify these effects or validate the inferred occluded geometry. Reusing the 50 m reconstruction for later lower-altitude captures also introduces acknowledged but unmeasured temporal mismatches.

The SSC experiment does not adequately establish a reliable baseline. Table 11 reports overall mIoU of 0.0080 (0.80%) and occupancy IoU of 0.2406, with numerous classes receiving zero IoU. Low performance can make a benchmark valuable, but with only CGFormer and no diagnostic controls—such as ground-truth depth, a simple projection baseline, or visible-versus-occluded evaluation—the results do not distinguish aerial task difficulty from adaptation problems, depth errors, or annotation issues. The claim that CGFormer is well suited under near-uniform class distributions is not demonstrated by these experiments.

Dataset diversity is narrower than the frame count suggests. There are nine scenes in one geographic region, and the test split contains only two urban/industrial scenes, without rural, summer, or winter coverage. Building voxels constitute 75.75% of labeled occupancy, while several advertised categories are extremely rare. Furthermore, altitude subsets have different scene mixtures: the two test scenes contribute 389/241 frames at 30 m versus 188/1,292 at 50 m. Consequently, the aggregate altitude comparisons cannot isolate altitude effects from scene composition.

Some experimental conclusions exceed their evidence. Table 10 compares reciprocal transfers evaluated on different target datasets, so lower absolute errors do not establish superior cross-domain generalization or downstream suitability. The annotation-efficiency evidence also lacks annotation time and a measured 3D-labeling comparator. These issues are secondary to ground-truth validity, but weaken the broader claims. Overall, the resource has worthwhile potential, yet uncertainty about annotation reliability and the unexplained SSC baseline failure currently outweigh the evidence for acceptance.

strengths: OccuFly addresses a valuable gap: real-world aerial semantic scene completion. Its 20,160 image–occupancy–depth samples, 22 semantic classes, and coverage of multiple altitudes, seasons, and environments could support useful research beyond terrestrial perception.

The camera-only annotation pipeline is practical and coherently described. Combining reconstruction, sparse 2D annotation, label lifting, and class-aware densification reduces direct 3D annotation requirements. Table 8 documents 586 manually annotated images among 6,393 reconstruction images.

The manuscript provides scene-disjoint training, validation, and test splits, class-wise results, qualitative examples, and substantial implementation details, including clustering parameters, reconstruction settings, and computational requirements.

The depth estimation experiments demonstrate concrete utility of the dataset's supervision. In Table 4, OccuFly-trained Depth Anything V2 substantially improves every reported metric over the terrestrial model at all three altitudes; for example, 30 m AbsRel decreases from 0.737 to 0.103.
weaknesses: The central benchmark ground truth is insufficiently validated. The reported 1.24-pixel reprojection error measures internal image consistency, not independent metric depth accuracy, semantic correctness, or volumetric completeness. No quantitative audit against independently measured geometry or manually verified 3D labels establishes the accuracy of the final evaluation targets. This is consequential because the dataset, rather than a new prediction method, is the primary contribution.

The treatment of unobserved geometry can introduce systematic evaluation errors. Instance silhouettes are synthesized from the same incomplete reconstructed point cloud, so carving cannot independently verify missing geometry; Poisson reconstruction likewise introduces inferred surfaces. Equation 13 labels remaining voxels empty, while the invalid mask excludes only regions outside the viewing frustum. The manuscript does not establish how genuinely unknown regions inside the frustum are distinguished from verified free space. Cross-altitude temporal inconsistencies are acknowledged but not quantified or filtered.

The SSC baseline does not yet establish a dependable interpretation of benchmark difficulty. Table 11 reports overall mIoU of 0.0080 (0.8%) and occupancy IoU of 0.2406, with many classes at zero. Low performance alone is not a weakness, but without a simple reference baseline, ground-truth-depth diagnostic, or adaptation checks, it remains unclear how much reflects aerial reasoning difficulty versus depth errors, label issues, or model adaptation. The claim that CGFormer is well suited to near-uniform class distributions is not supported by an experiment with such distributions.

The apparent scale exceeds the diversity of independent evaluation environments: all data come from nine scenes in one geographic region, and the test split contains only two scenes, with no rural scene. Buildings account for 75.75% of labeled occupancy, whereas people and flying animals are nearly absent. Consequently, broad claims about seasonal robustness and fine-grained 22-class evaluation need qualification; frame count does not compensate for limited independent scene and rare-class coverage.

Several supporting claims exceed the reported evidence. The claim that fewer than 10% of images per scene require annotation conflicts with Table 8, where five scenes require approximately 13.7–17.3%; only the pooled ratio is below 10%. The cross-domain superiority argument in Section 9.2 compares errors on different target datasets, and AbsRel actually worsens from 0.729 to 1.098. These are correctable interpretation issues, but the more material ground-truth validation and baseline-diagnostic gaps currently tip the overall balance toward weak rejection despite the dataset's worthwhile premise.

strengths: OccuFly addresses a valuable gap in aerial 3D perception. The combination of 20,611 image–occupancy–depth samples, 21 semantic classes, multiple altitudes, and geographically disjoint scene splits could support useful research beyond adapting terrestrial SSC benchmarks.

The camera-based annotation pipeline is practically motivated and reasonably well described. Combining photogrammetric reconstruction, sparse 2D annotation, multi-view label fusion, and class-aware densification reduces reliance on manual 3D labeling. Table 9 reports 586 annotated images out of 6,393 reconstruction images, supporting the aggregate 9.17% annotation ratio.

The authors provide meaningful quality checks: evaluation against 135 additional annotated images yields 92% pixel agreement, and the supplement includes scene-wise reconstructions, reprojection errors, annotation statistics, and several implementation parameters. These support visible-surface consistency, although they do not fully validate completed occupancy.

The depth experiments demonstrate practical value from in-domain supervision. Fine-tuning DepthAnything2 improves AbsRel from 0.729 to 0.134 and RMSE from 28.382 to 4.844 on the held-out test scenes. The SSC experiments also include two established methods and detailed class-wise results.
weaknesses: The central concern is insufficient validation of the final 3D ground truth. The 92% agreement evaluates rendered semantic point clouds, rather than the completed voxel labels produced by visual-hull carving and Poisson reconstruction. Likewise, a 1.24-pixel reprojection error measures image consistency, not absolute metric accuracy or correctness of hidden geometry. Silhouettes generated from the reconstructed point cloud cannot independently verify missing surfaces or concavities. A quantitative audit of final occupancy, including occluded regions and class-wise label accuracy, is needed to substantiate the benchmark's principal target.

The treatment of unknown space risks systematic evaluation errors. Equation (13) assigns empty labels everywhere outside the reconstructed or densified occupancy, while Equation (14) invalidates only voxels outside the camera frustum. Consequently, regions unobserved across the acquisition can become supervised empty space rather than unknown space. The manuscript does not quantify this issue or distinguish observed free space from reconstruction failures. This is particularly consequential for completion, where hidden geometry is the target.

The reported SSC metric is inconsistent with the class-wise results. In Table 11, DISC's 21 class IoUs sum to 38.75, giving approximately 1.85% mIoU rather than 2.04%; Symphonies similarly gives approximately 0.53% rather than 0.58%. Both reported values match division by 19 rather than 21. No exclusion of two semantic classes is documented. This may be correctable, but it leaves the benchmark's evaluation protocol uncertain.

The extremely low SSC performance is not sufficiently diagnosed. Even with an adapted depth estimator, the methods achieve only 0.58% and 2.04% reported mIoU, with numerous classes never recovered. The paper provides no ground-truth-depth diagnostic, simple projection baseline, or convergence evidence to distinguish genuine task difficulty from depth sensitivity or adaptation problems. The supplement gives hardware and batch size but omits the actual training schedules and important input/calibration adaptation details. Low performance alone is not a weakness; the unresolved explanation limits the benchmark's interpretability.

The apparent scale exceeds the diversity of independent environments: all data come from nine scenes around one city, and the test split contains only two scenes, with no rural scene. Building voxels constitute 75.75% of the test distribution, while several classes are extremely rare. The dataset remains useful, but aggregate agreement and frame counts provide limited evidence for broad semantic or seasonal robustness.

The recommendation favors rejection because uncertainty about completed-label validity and the evaluation protocol affects the core benchmark contribution. The useful dataset concept, annotation efficiency, and depth adaptation results are substantial merits, but they do not resolve those central reliability concerns.

strengths: OccuFly addresses a meaningful gap in aerial semantic scene completion. Its 20,611 image–occupancy–depth samples, 21 semantic classes, and geographically disjoint scene splits could provide a useful resource beyond existing terrestrial benchmarks.

The camera-based annotation pipeline is practical: photogrammetric reconstruction, sparse manual image annotation, and multi-view label transfer reduce direct 3D annotation effort. Table 9 documents 586 annotated acquisition images out of 6,393, supporting the aggregate 9.17% annotation ratio.

The 92% pixel agreement against 135 additional manually annotated images provides useful independent evidence for projected semantic quality. Scene-level visualizations also show coherent reconstructed layouts.

Depth fine-tuning demonstrates concrete utility: DepthAnything2 improves from 0.729 to 0.134 AbsRel and from 28.382 to 4.844 RMSE on the test set. The supplementary material supplies class-wise results and several important reconstruction parameters.
weaknesses: The principal concern is insufficient validation of the final 3D benchmark targets. The 1.24-pixel reprojection error measures image consistency, not independently verified metric scale or depth accuracy. Likewise, the 92% agreement evaluates rendered semantic point clouds, rather than the final densified occupancy volumes, and lacks class-wise accuracy and coverage details. Consequently, these checks do not establish the accuracy of the occluded geometry central to SSC.

The target-generation procedure introduces consequential, unquantified assumptions. Section 3.3.3 constructs silhouettes from the reconstructed points themselves, so virtual views supply no independent evidence about missing surfaces. Visual-hull filling and Poisson reconstruction can introduce unsupported occupancy. Equation (13) labels remaining voxels empty, while Equation (14) invalidates only regions outside the current frustum; no explicit reconstruction-unknown mask is described. Missing geometry can therefore become evaluated free space. No quantitative densification ablation or final-volume audit establishes the impact.

The SSC experiments do not sufficiently diagnose their extremely low semantic performance: Symphonies and DISC obtain only 0.58% and 2.04% mIoU. Low scores alone are not a weakness of a challenging dataset, but here an oracle-depth experiment, simple semantic lifting baseline, or training/convergence analysis is needed to distinguish task difficulty from depth errors and adaptation problems. The fine-tuned depth estimator still has 4.844 m RMSE against a 0.5 m voxel size. The reported results therefore provide limited support for attributing failure broadly to aerial semantic understanding.

Reproducibility is incomplete for the benchmark adaptations. Section 8 specifies official implementations, hardware, batch size, and grid dimensions, but omits training duration, optimization settings, image preprocessing, and detailed camera-to-grid adaptation. These choices are especially relevant when interpreting near-zero semantic scores and metric-scale failures.

The breadth claims exceed the independent evaluation coverage. All nine scenes come from one geographic region, and the test set contains only two scenes, with no rural, winter, or summer test scene. Buildings constitute 75.75% of test occupied voxels, while several classes are extremely rare. This does not negate the dataset's usefulness, but limits claims of broad robustness and reliable evaluation across all 21 classes.

Several correctable reporting errors weaken interpretation: Section 4.3 claims fewer than 10% annotated images per scene despite Table 9 reporting 13.68–17.34% for five scenes; Section 5.2 claims SILog degrades after fine-tuning although both fine-tuned models improve in Table 5. These are secondary to the ground-truth and benchmark-validation concerns, which determine the weak-reject recommendation despite the resource's worthwhile potential.

strengths: OccuFly addresses a meaningful gap: real-world aerial semantic scene completion. Its 20,611 image–occupancy–depth samples, 21 semantic classes, multiple altitudes, and scene-disjoint splits could support useful research beyond terrestrial driving benchmarks.

The camera-based annotation pipeline is a practical contribution. Combining photogrammetric reconstruction, sparse manual image annotation, label lifting, and class-aware densification reduces the need for direct 3D annotation. Table 9 documents 586 annotated images out of 6,393 reconstruction images, supporting the aggregate annotation-efficiency claim.

The evaluation includes useful evidence of label consistency: 135 additional manually annotated views, excluded from label generation, achieve 92% pixel-wise agreement with rendered semantic point clouds. Scene-level visualizations also make the generated data reasonably inspectable.

The depth experiments demonstrate concrete utility. Fine-tuning DepthAnything2 improves AbsRel from 0.729 to 0.134 and δ1 from 0.002 to 0.834 on the held-out test set. Benchmarking two SSC methods and four depth models provides useful starting points.

The manuscript clearly describes the major pipeline components, supplies several implementation parameters in the supplement, and explicitly acknowledges static-scene assumptions and temporal inconsistencies across altitude captures.
weaknesses: The principal concern is validation of the final occupancy targets. The 92% agreement evaluates projected semantic point clouds, not the subsequently densified voxel grids or their hidden geometry. Reprojection error of 1.24 pixels establishes image-space consistency but does not independently establish metric scale or depth accuracy. Thus, the evidence supports visible semantic alignment more strongly than the claimed accuracy of the full 3D ground truth.

The treatment of unknown space is insufficiently justified. Equation (13) assigns empty labels wherever reconstructed or densified occupancy is absent, while the invalid mask excludes only voxels outside the frustum. Unobserved regions within the frustum can therefore become empty targets without evidence of free space. Virtual-view silhouette carving and Poisson reconstruction additionally impose geometric assumptions whose errors are not quantified. These choices materially affect an SSC benchmark’s evaluation targets.

The SSC results remain difficult to interpret: Symphonies and DISC achieve only 0.58% and 2.04% mIoU, respectively, with many classes effectively unrecovered. Low performance alone is not a weakness, but the manuscript provides insufficient diagnostic evidence to distinguish aerial task difficulty from depth-prior errors, training/adaptation problems, or target construction. A ground-truth-depth diagnostic or simple projection baseline is absent, and the reported training details omit important optimization and adaptation settings.

The breadth implied by the sample count exceeds the breadth of independent environments. All nine scenes are from the Ingolstadt region, and the test set comprises only two scenes, with no rural test scene. Its occupied-voxel distribution is approximately 75.75% building (Table 11), while several classes are extremely rare. This limits conclusions about general aerial SSC, seasonal robustness, and the utility of the full taxonomy.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in the interpretation, although they are secondary to ground-truth validity. Section 4.3 claims fewer than 10% annotations per scene, whereas Table 9 shows five scenes above 10%; only the aggregate claim is supported. Section 5.2 claims SILog deteriorates after fine-tuning, but Table 5 shows improvement for both fine-tuned models. The relationship between 6,393 acquired reconstruction images and 20,611 final samples also needs a clearer accounting.

Overall, the new aerial resource and demonstrated depth-estimation utility place the paper near the acceptance boundary. However, uncertainty about unobserved-space labels, densified geometry, and the interpretation of the SSC baselines prevents a confident acceptance recommendation for the benchmark as currently validated.
